stances.claim: Prior column 'Scotus legalizes bribery' drew 'a record number of applauses (and some applesauce)' across emails, texts, and calls -- including a Google top-news placement (NYC, July 29) alongside The Guardian and Chicago Tribune that 'catapulted the Inquirer among the most respected British and US dailies.'

Gallup's July 30 report confirms 'Approval of US Supreme Court Stalled Near Historic Low' -- highest rating 62% (2000, 2001); below 50% from 2011-2017; majorities again 2018-2020 during Trump's three appointments; below 50% since 2023-2024 term.

Retired PH SC colleagues uniformly condemn the Snyder decision: J Carpio -- 'utterly shameful and morally bankrupt. What cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. Those Scotus justices are announcing publicly that they expect to collect gratuities after they retire'; J Sandoval-Gutierrez -- 'flabbergasted and shocked. This is not the Court we knew. Sadly, the sterling Justices we visited and admired have retired.'

To be fair, lone Scotus defender J Vicente V. Mendoza (Yale alumnus) reasoned that 'the real question or gravamen of the crime here may not really be whether payment was given before or after the subject of the crime' -- post-act payments of $5,000+ may be tokens lacking 'corrupt state of mind.'

Cross-sector reactions: Dean Nilo Divina -- 'I concur with nary a dissent, CJ'; Edgardo Lacson -- 'shocking... politically silly and kindergarten decision... the BEST JUSTICES MONEY CAN BUY'; Dr. Jose Acuin (Taglish) -- 'Hindi ka pwedeng sumuntok pag may nakatago sa kilikili mo' (you can't throw a punch when you have something hidden in your armpit) -- confirming convergence across academe, business, and medical sectors.

President Biden's July 29 three-point Scotus-reform proposal -- (1) constitutional amendment establishing no immunity for in-office presidential crimes, (2) 18-year term limits with biennial appointments, (3) binding code of conduct requiring gift disclosure, prohibiting public political activity, and mandating recusal for financial/spousal conflicts -- needs US Congress support with uncertainty whether the 'lame-duck' Congress will follow.

CJ wrote the three columns 'not to degrade the Scotus further into the abyss but to entice it to levitate itself. I merely stated the facts and the truth, for the truth shall set the Scotus free to climb anew to its former Olympian heights that I used to look up to.'

Closing prayer: 'I firmly believe that justice is blind and that justices must be beyond reproach. My prayer is for the Scotus to rise like the Phoenix and become again the indisputable cradle of the rule of law and the unblemished judicial standard for all freedom-loving countries.'

one_paragraph_summary: CJ reports that his July 29 column 'Scotus legalizes bribery' drew 'a record number of applauses (and some applesauce)' via emails, texts, and calls from the Philippines and abroad -- even rating a full column from Manila Overseas Press Club prexy Tony Lopez ('The decline of Scotus,' Philippine Star, 6/18/24). An anonymous NYC reader sent a screenshot of Google top news in the US on July 29 at 10:30 AM NYC time showing CJ's column and portrait alongside The Guardian and the Chicago Tribune's 'Ex-AT&T boss accused of bribing Michael Madigan,' 'catapulting the Inquirer among the most respected British and US dailies.' Another US reader emailed a July 30 Gallup report -- 'Approval of US Supreme Court Stalled Near Historic Low' -- tracing Scotus approval from a high of 62% (2000, 2001) to below 50% from 2011-2017, back to majority approval 2018-2020 during Trump's three appointments, then below 50% since the 2023-2024 term. CJ quotes retired PH SC colleagues. J Antonio T. Carpio: 'This Scotus decision is utterly shameful and morally bankrupt. What cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. Those Scotus justices are announcing publicly that they expect to collect gratuities after they retire. All US government officials can also expect the same gratuities.' J Angelina Sandoval-Gutierrez, who heads the PH SC's Judicial Integrity Board (which investigates judicial misconduct in all courts except the SC, which has its own ethics committee): 'Chief, I am also flabbergasted and shocked. This is not the Court we knew. Sadly, the sterling Justices we visited and admired have retired.' To be fair, CJ quotes 'the lone Scotus defender,' Yale alumnus J Vicente V. Mendoza: 'The real question or gravamen of the crime here may not really be whether payment was given before or after the subject of the crime. The Court held that those given before are inherently bribes but those amounting to 5,000 dollars or more which are given after may only be tokens [of] appreciation and do not per se show a corrupt state of mind. In the case in question, the transaction was worth 1.1 million dollars but the payment to the mayor was only 13,000 dollars [that] may not really show corrupt intent.' Cross-sector reactions follow: Dean Nilo Divina -- 'I concur with nary a dissent, CJ'; former PCCI president Edgardo Lacson -- 'shocking indeed to know the Scotus distinguished bribery and gratuity by a timeline... politically silly and kindergarten decision... the BEST JUSTICES MONEY CAN BUY'; Dr. Jose Acuin in Taglish -- 'Hindi ka pwedeng sumuntok pag may nakatago sa kilikili mo' (you can't throw a punch when you have something hidden in your armpit). CJ then recites President Biden's July 29 three measures: (1) a constitutional amendment ensuring no immunity for in-office presidential crimes; (2) Scotus term limits with the President appointing a Justice every two years to serve 18 years in active service; (3) a binding Code of Conduct requiring gift disclosure, prohibiting public political activity, and mandating recusal for financial or spousal conflicts. Whether 'lame-duck' US Congress will follow remains uncertain. CJ closes: 'I wrote my three columns not to degrade the Scotus further into the abyss but to entice it to levitate itself. I merely stated the facts and the truth, for the truth shall set the Scotus free to climb anew to its former Olympian heights that I used to look up to. At bottom, I firmly believe that justice is blind and that justices must be beyond reproach. My prayer is for the Scotus to rise like the Phoenix and become again the indisputable cradle of the rule of law and the unblemished judicial standard for all freedom-loving countries.'
